evidence.section_title: Trapped in transition: findings from a UK study of student suicide
evidence.quote: [/page/1/Text/6] This study of student suicide within UK higher education directs attention to the community context of suicide.

The qualitative study of student suicide reported here aimed to engage higher UK education institutions (HEIs) in suicide prevention by identifying approaches and strategies which were within the remit of a learning organisation and achievable.

[/page/4/Text/6] All HEIs in the UK were invited to identify relevant cases for the study and 24 HEIs reported cases that met the study criteria and where staff (usually the Head of Counselling Services) felt able to assist the researchers by making the initial contact with families of students who had died. Coroners in England and Procurators Fiscal in Scotland also assisted in finding relevant cases for inclusion in the research.
However, the sample did include student deaths from a wide range of HEIs across the UK.

evidence.section_title: Risk factors specific to student life
evidence.quote: ... his worst thing was failure, he hated failure, and I suppose failing first year at uni was obviously a massive trigger ... (Student friend W100).

The findings on academic failure paint a picture of students seeking an escape from what was experienced as an increasingly intolerable state of existence where the prospect of failure loomed large. Transitional periods in the academic year appeared key in providing a context for this state of mind. Three-quarters of the deaths occurred either at the beginning or at the end of the academic year. Parents' and friends' accounts described the inner psychic experience of the students as mirroring this external context of transition.

Interviews with family and friends inevitably rely on their perceptions and reconstructions of the state of mind of the person who died. These reconstructions are then filtered through the researchers' perspectives and preoccupations (Denzin & Lincoln, 2003). However, this study used a range of informants to develop a complex multi-dimensional account of the events and circumstances surrounding student suicides.

evidence.section_title: Trapped in transition: findings from a UK study of student suicide
evidence.quote: [/page/1/Text/6] A modified psychological autopsy approach was used to explore 20 case studies of student suicide from the period 2000–2005, drawing on the perspectives of family members, friends and university staff.

The qualitative study of student suicide reported here aimed to engage higher UK education institutions (HEIs) in suicide prevention by identifying approaches and strategies which were within the remit of a learning organisation and achievable.

The research built on the psychological autopsy approach (Beskow, Runeson, & Asgard, 1990) which aims to collect data surrounding an individual death in order to explain it. The study described here, known as the RaPSS study (Responses and Prevention in Student Suicide), which was undertaken between 2004 and 2006, took a primarily qualitative approach. It focused on the immediate and current environment of the young people who died: that is, the HEI setting and the HEI community, its structures and resources, were seen as providing a relevant context for the deaths studied. The research aimed to draw together a range of accounts of the young person's death and its impact, acknowledging that the knowledge held by different informants was partial and limited.

[/page/4/Text/7] Once consent had been obtained, interviews were undertaken with a parent or parents, students' friends and academic or student support staff who had known the student well. Copies of the relevant Coroners' or Procurators Fiscals' records were also acquired. Between two and six data sources were collected for each of the case studies with a total number of 73 sources of data being collated. [/page/4/Text/8] Interviews were undertaken using a semi-structured schedule and were recorded and transcribed with permission.

evidence.section_title: Trapped in transition: findings from a UK study of student suicide
evidence.quote: [/page/1/Text/6] The study identifies features of the higher education community salient for suicide prevention and concludes that the concept of transition is useful in considering the potential interaction across time and place of the risk factors for vulnerable students.

[/page/5/Text/9] Data analysis identified a multiplicity of risk factors in the lives of the young people who died. In virtually all the case studies, these risk factors occurred in combination. Here they are discussed under three broad headings. The first of these concerns risk factors that were located in the individuals and their behaviour. These include mental health problems, substance misuse, previous suicidal behaviour and talk, self-harm, and perfectionism. The second group of factors focuses on social networks and [/page/6/Text/3] includes students' relationships and the transmission of suicidal behaviour. These are widely recognised risk factors for suicide but they may be heightened in education settings where students are particularly reliant on the network of friendships and contacts which student life offers. The third group includes factors specific to student life including academic progress and transitional periods in the academic year.

[/page/6/Text/5] 14 of the 20 students had been diagnosed with a mental health problem at the time of their death. [/page/6/Text/6] Students' friends reported that the stigma attached to mental health problems had been a further disincentive to seeking help for some: [/page/7/Text/2] exacerbate depression. Likewise, heavy cannabis use in three cases was associated with both alcohol problems and depression. [/page/7/Text/3] Seven students were reported to have previously attempted suicide, although not all had received hospital treatment or were perceived to making a serious attempt at the time. [/page/7/Text/5] Perfectionism was another characteristic which appeared prevalent and a relationship between perfectionism and suicide has been identified by other studies (Blatt, 1995; Hunter & O'Connor, 2003). 11 students were described as perfectionists or as having an extreme fear of failure:

evidence.section_title: Relationships and networks in the HE community
evidence.quote: Six of the students had experienced the break-up of a relationship shortly before their death; three were experiencing difficulties in a relationship and a further three students were described as experiencing unrequited love. A number of these relationships were described by friends or parents as 'turbulent' or 'emotionally charged'. Informants conveyed a picture of young people with limited experiences of intimate relationships struggling to manage the emotional vulnerability and losses they experienced: Two of the students who died had expressed doubts about their sexuality and these appeared to be a major source of uncertainty and distress for them. Suicide transmission (the term is used here in preference to the term 'suicide contagion') was a feature of four of the case study deaths. In two cases, the deaths of students included in the study occurred soon after or close to the anniversary of the suicide of a close friend. In another case, a friend of the student who was included in the research took their own life soon after: using the same method of death. In the fourth case, the student who died had had a relationship with another student who was described as attempting to take her own life on a number of occasions.

evidence.section_title: Risk factors specific to student life
evidence.quote: HE is structured around a series of academic hurdles. Assessment is no longer confined to final exams but is recurs throughout the academic year providing multiple opportunities for failure in the HE experience. Half the students had a history of disrupted or failing academic careers. In retrospect, these changes in programme and suspensions of study appeared to be indicators of an increasing inability to manage the demands of university life.

The findings on academic failure paint a picture of students seeking an escape from what was experienced as an increasingly intolerable state of existence where the prospect of failure loomed large. Transitional periods in the academic year appeared key in providing a context for this state of mind. Parents' and friends' accounts described the inner psychic experience of the students as mirroring this external context of transition. The data depicted a state of mind which saw no prospect of returning to the previous year's existence but which characterised the future as threatening further failures: These transitional periods at the beginnings and ends of the academic year appeared to provide a context which fed into the students'sense of being trapped in a position that they found unendurable. ... The students in this study seemed, from the accounts of those who had known them well, to be seeking an escape from what they experienced as an intolerable situation and to be opting for suicide as a means of avoiding further failure and distress.

[/page/10/Text/6] However, this study is concerned less with highlighting the risks posed by particular months in the academic year but rather seeks to emphasise the transitional nature of the periods of vulnerability identified. Transitional periods appear to deprive students of established sources of support while compelling them to contemplate future demands and pressures. For those who are already vulnerable as a result of mental health problems, substance misuse, perfectionist tendencies or life events such as a relationship breakdown or the suicide of a friend, the synchronicity of such risks may be particularly telling in such periods.

In the UK, the Social Exclusion Unit (Office of the Deputy Prime Minister, 2005) has drawn attention to the transitional experience of young adulthood and the risks this entails for young people experiencing high levels of deprivation in combination with other needs. However, this study of student suicide suggests that the risks associated with transition can be high even for more affluent groups of young people in the relatively sheltered setting of HE. Within this broad context of transition, the sense of being 'inbetween' may be heightened at the start and finish of the academic year. The experience of transition may weaken support networks whilst exposing students with existing vulnerabilities to heightened fears about the future. The participants in this study characterised the response to this experience of transition as a state of entrapment from which suicide was conceptualised as a release.
